approachQuestion.prompt:
Combine two sparse measurements

Input: arrays left and right of (coordinate,value) records representing sparse integer vectors. Each coordinate occurs at most once within each array, records are unsorted, and omitted coordinates have value zero. Return the dot product: sum of leftValue×rightValue over coordinates present in both.

Example 1: left = [(2,3),(8,−2)], right = [(8,4),(5,7),(2,6)]. Output: 10. Example 2: left = [], right = [(4,9)]. Output: 0. Both lengths are between 0 and 200,000; coordinates are integers from 0 to 1,000,000,000; absolute values are at most 1,000, ensuring the sum fits signed 64-bit arithmetic.

Constraints: input is immutable; all identifiers and numeric entries are signed 32-bit integers unless specified. Arithmetic uses signed 64-bit integers. Prefer the least expected running-time growth, then avoid unnecessary asymptotic auxiliary storage. Non-adversarial hashing of fixed-size integer keys/tuples has expected amortized constant cost.

options.text: Build a coordinate-to-value map for the shorter array. Scan the longer array, adding the product whenever its coordinate is found in the map.
options.feedback: Uniqueness within each input means each matched coordinate contributes exactly once. Indexing the shorter side keeps auxiliary storage tied to its size.

options.text: Build a coordinate-to-value map for the longer array and scan the shorter one.
options.feedback: This computes the same sum with equivalent expected time, but can use avoidably more memory when one array is much shorter.

options.text: Comparison-sort copies of both arrays by coordinate and merge matching records.
options.feedback: Sorted merging is correct, but ordering both arrays adds removable work and copies.

options.text: Multiply records at matching array positions, ignoring coordinates.
options.feedback: For left [(2,3)] and right [(8,4),(2,6)], the answer is 18; multiplying the first records gives 12.

feedback.reason: Join sparse data by a key and index the smaller side instead of allocating the coordinate universe.
details: Build a map from every coordinate in the shorter array to its value. Scan the longer array and add the product for each coordinate found. If either input is empty, return zero immediately.
Only matching coordinates contribute products. Index the smaller sparse list; the coordinate universe may be much larger than either stored list, so a dense array would add irrelevant storage.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method “Combine two sparse measurements — analyzed method”, n = left.length and m = right.length. State the standard worst-input bound by total supplied size; an empty-side input can return earlier. Choose its time and auxiliary-space pair. Use the tightest standard bound for the worst legal input for the stated size parameters, with expected time over non-adversarial hashing. Fixed-width integer and fixed-size tuple hash operations take expected amortized O(1); arithmetic, comparison and copying one integer take O(1). Auxiliary space excludes the supplied input and returned result, includes all maps, sets, temporary copies and call stacks. The method is iterative, with constant call-stack space.

For nonempty inputs, inserting min(n,m) records and scanning max(n,m) records takes expected O(n+m). With an empty side the method returns immediately; O(n+m+1) is the tight standard worst-input bound by total size.
O(min(n,m)+1) for the smaller-side map and scalar state. Inputs and scalar result are excluded; there are no copies.
“Expected O(n + m + 1) worst-input time; O(min(n,m) + 1) auxiliary space.”: Correct under the stated expected/amortized hashing model.
“Expected O(nm + 1) time; O(1) space.”: The fixed method uses coordinate lookups rather than comparing every record pair.
“Expected O(n + m + 1) time; O(max(n,m) + 1) space as the tight bound.”: It indexes the shorter input; the larger-side bound is avoidably loose for this method.
“Expected O(n + m + 1) time; O(1) space.”: When both inputs are nonempty, a map of the smaller input is retained.
